item.title: Re: Why is the time significant?
item.content:encoded: GMT is a time zone in England (Greenwich Mean Time), so 3 A.M. GMT would be (for example) 10 P.M. in New York city or 6 P.M. in California.

item.title: Why is the time significant?
item.content:encoded: It's described as turning on at 3am GMT but that's just an arbritary time to describe, as 3am is many different times. Does it turn on at 3am wherever it is?

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
And as for containment worthiness, there's the security risk inherent in this thing randomly broadcasting any location, secret or not.

That was my main reason for containment. I consider the event captured in 461-1 to be a secondary effect.

Perhaps ironically, the Foundation may have opened itself up to operational risk by obtaining SCP-461, since the device now appears to "know" about them and the facility it's contained in. However, the risk is relatively mild, since SCP-461 only activates for five minutes at a time and appears to draw from a large "database" of footage, making it a pretty unreliable spying tool. Still, it's enough to justify containment, never mind the protection of other national security assets unrelated to the Foundation. There's also the possibility of SCP-461 revealing information that no one is prepared to know…

At any rate, I wonder if I should clarify that there is a Foundation-supplied VCR hooked into SCP-461 and recording its footage?

That feels like the lead in to a horror movie scene, and the fact that there's no specific call out to anything terrible happening in this article makes me worry that much more.

And as for containment worthiness, there's the security risk inherent in this thing randomly broadcasting any location, secret or not.

"Today, the device displayed footage of the interior of the room it is contained in, from the perspective of the corner just above the door. However, there are no security cameras or other video recording devices in the room. Advise that no fewer than two individuals occupy the room at one time. Also advise closed-circuit cameras to be installed in the room to monitor for unusual phenomena."

what immediately amused me with this was the possibility of it pulling footage from the future, from cameras they put in, recording people that they said should be in there, that all happened because they found the footage in the first place

anyway fun article, and my only gripe is that i dont see anything about it that would make them qualify it as an SCP object per se rather than an anomalous object, it doesnt appear to be something that really requires containment outside of keeping it away from the public eye where it'd become a major scientific curiosity

I like the mild paranoia this one would cause in-universe, as it's implied that it can display anything, anywhere.
The ending, however, is iffy in my opinion. On one hand it's open-ended enough that people finish on an intriguing train of thought, but on the other it feels like it could be better, creepier, if you fleshed it out. But, the atypical ending is what really makes this memorable, so I'd say to leave it as it is.

I'm pretty curious as to what others think the guy in the corner actually was. My first thought was that the perspective of the TV follows the general perspective of the guy. Which means that he wanders around wherever, as nobody can see him. Watching.

item.content:encoded:
I strongly approve.

I love that it looks like an ongoing document rather than the results of long term research. The unanswered questions offered by the second and third notes lead to far more interesting places in the mind of the reader than anything you could possibly write. Now that you've gotten that far, though, temptation to ruin the delicate balance you've achieved will come in the form of comments asking for clarification.

My advice: ignore anything anyone tells you to add to this page. It's excellent as-is. Like I said, at this point anything you add can only detract from the spirit of the piece.

(Ignore sophos. I usually do. It's not boring.)

Do consider italicizing the researcher's notes, though. Addenda are in italics throughout the site, and there's no harm in fitting in.
